item.title: Powering the AI Boom: Why Data Centers Are Showing Up on Your Electric Bill
item.body:
Electricity used to be one of the most predictable lines in a household budget. In many parts of the United States, that is changing. Retail power prices have risen faster than general inflation in recent years, and the rapid growth of data centers, the facilities that run cloud computing and artificial intelligence, is one of the reasons analysts and regulators keep pointing to. This explainer walks through how that cost can travel from a server hall to a monthly bill, and what policymakers are doing about it.

*This article is for general information only and is not financial or legal advice. Figures are approximate and vary by region and year.*

## Why data centers matter to the grid

For about fifteen years, U.S. electricity demand was nearly flat, because efficiency gains offset population and economic growth. Utilities and grid operators planned around that stability.

Large data centers break that pattern. A single big campus can require as much power as a small city, and it can ask for that power within a few years. Grid planners in several regions, including parts of Virginia, Texas, Ohio, Georgia and the Mid-Atlantic, have sharply raised their demand forecasts. Power plants and transmission lines, by contrast, take years to permit and build.

When demand grows faster than supply, power becomes scarcer and costlier. That is the basic economic pressure behind the headlines.

## Not every price increase is caused by data centers

It is worth being careful here. Electric bills rise for many reasons:

- **Natural gas prices**, which set wholesale power prices in many markets.
- **Aging infrastructure** that utilities must repair or replace.
- **Wildfire, storm and resilience spending**, especially in some western and coastal states.
- **Transmission upgrades** to connect new generation, including renewables.
- **General inflation** in labor and equipment.

Data center demand is one factor among several, and its share differs from place to place. Studies from grid operators, consultants and consumer advocates reach different conclusions about how much it contributes. Treat any single number with caution.

## Channel one: capacity auctions

In some regions, grid operators run auctions to make sure enough power plants will be available in future years, even if they only run at peak times. The best-known example is PJM Interconnection, which serves 13 states and Washington, D.C., from Illinois to New Jersey.

Here is how it works in simple terms:

1. The grid operator forecasts peak demand for a future delivery year.
2. Power plant owners and demand-response providers bid to promise their availability.
3. The auction sets a single clearing price, usually quoted in dollars per megawatt-day, that all accepted resources receive.
4. Utilities, and the retail suppliers that serve customers, pay those costs and generally pass them through to customers.

When forecast demand rises and supply is tight, clearing prices rise. PJM's auction for the 2025/26 delivery year cleared at roughly $270 per megawatt-day, up from about $29 the year before. Later auctions for 2026/27 and 2027/28 cleared at the maximum price allowed under a temporary cap-and-floor arrangement, around $329 and $333 per megawatt-day. PJM and independent market monitors have cited data center load growth as a significant driver of the higher forecasts.

Because these charges are folded into bills as contracts and rates roll over, households often see the effect months after an auction, and in steps rather than all at once.

## Channel two: utility rate cases

The second path runs through state utility regulators. Most households buy power from a regulated utility whose prices are set in a **rate case**, a formal proceeding in which the utility asks a public utility commission to approve the revenue it needs.

Utilities earn a regulated return on the infrastructure they build, so new substations, transmission lines and generation can raise the revenue requirement. If a utility builds for data center demand, the question becomes who pays:

- If the data center pays for the full cost of serving it, other customers are largely protected.
- If costs are spread across all customers, and the expected data center load is delayed, smaller than promised, or leaves, ordinary ratepayers may be stuck with a share of the bill.

That second scenario is the central worry. Regulators call it the risk of **stranded costs**, and consumer advocates argue it is a real risk because tech companies can change plans faster than a 30-year power plant can be retired.

## What regulators and states are doing

Policymakers have responded in several ways, and the approaches are still evolving.

**Special rate classes for large users.** A number of states have approved or are considering tariffs for very large customers. Typical features include long contract terms of 10 to 20 years, minimum monthly charges that apply whether or not the customer uses the power ("take-or-pay"), exit fees, and collateral requirements. Ohio, Indiana, Georgia, Virginia and others have taken steps in this direction.

**Making large users bring their own power.** Some proposals encourage or require data centers to fund new generation, sign power purchase agreements, or use on-site generation, so that new demand comes with new supply.

**Wholesale market reforms.** At the federal level, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission has been examining how large loads connect to the grid and how costs are assigned, including co-location of data centers at power plants. PJM has also been revising its auction rules and load forecasting, and its price cap and floor were negotiated with state officials after complaints from governors.

**Better forecasting and transparency.** Because developers sometimes file overlapping requests for the same power, regulators are asking for firmer commitments and clearer data so utilities do not overbuild.

**Efficiency and flexibility.** Some utilities and researchers are exploring whether data centers can reduce use during peak hours, which would ease strain and reduce the need for new plants.

## What households can do

You cannot control a capacity auction, but you can take practical steps:

- **Read your bill** to see the supply charge, delivery charge and any riders or surcharges.
- **Check whether you can choose a supplier.** In some states you can, but compare the price, contract length and fees carefully, and watch for teaser rates.
- **Ask about time-of-use plans** and efficiency rebates from your utility.
- **Weatherize and upgrade** insulation, thermostats and appliances, which lowers use regardless of the rate.
- **Participate.** Utility commissions hold public comment periods on rate cases, and comments from customers are part of the record.

## The bottom line

The artificial intelligence boom is real, and so is its appetite for electricity. Whether it raises household bills depends on decisions still being made: how costs are allocated, how fast new supply is built, and how much risk shifts to the companies that benefit. Data centers can also bring tax revenue, jobs and, in some cases, grid investment that benefits everyone. The policy debate is about making sure the costs and benefits are shared fairly.

*Sources worth checking for current numbers: your state public utility commission, PJM Interconnection and its independent market monitor, the U.S. Energy Information Administration, and the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission.*
